blocks.text: The rest of what Job says about the ostrich in chapter 39, verses 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21, is explained.

Now that we have explained in Job what was by far the most difficult point about the ostrich, [col. 250] in the rest there will be less labour and more profit. After the ἀκανθολογίαν [akanthologian], or gathering of thorns, will follow the ἀνθολογία [anthologia], or more truly the gleaning of ears. The sacred words run thus: But she leaves her eggs on the ground, and they are warmed upon the dust. And she forgets that the foot may crush them, and the beast of the field trample them. She deals harshly with her chicks, as if they were not hers. She has laboured in vain, she is without fear. For God has deprived her of wisdom, and has not imparted understanding to her. When she raises herself on high, she laughs at the horse and its rider. We shall now expound these one by one.

But she leaves her eggs on the ground] In Hebrew, כי תעזוב לארץ ביציה. The connection of this verse with the preceding one is as follows: "The ostrich exults in her wings, which she has swift and beautiful; but she is also ἄστοργος [astorgos], and neglects her eggs. She has some endowments of body, but a hard and pitiless mind." Thus כי in this place means the same as but, as in Gen. XLV, 8. It was not you who sent me here, כי האלהים, but God. She leaves, תעזוב, is an enallage of number. For the plural had preceded: The wing of the ostriches exults. But nothing is more frequent than this enallage in the book of Job. So in this very passage: She leaves her eggs on the ground, etc. And she forgets that the foot may tread on it. And a little below, of the horse: Have you given the horse strength, etc. They paw in the valley, and he rejoices in strength. The same verb תעזוב, she leaves, though feminine in gender, nevertheless refers to the noun רננים renanim, of masculine ending. But יענים, ostriches, יעלים, ibexes, רמכים, mares, רחלים, ewes, and in this very place ביצים, eggs, although of masculine ending, are nevertheless feminine in gender ^{(1)}. Further, the fact that this bird is said to leave her eggs on the ground plainly shows that it is the ostrich. For in the whole class of birds no other presents itself which is truly charged with this crime. The Indians, it is true, according to Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 13), hate swans because report has it that they ἐπιβουλεύειν ἐκγόνοις, καὶ διαφθείρειν τὰ ὠὰ [epibouleuein ekgonois, kai diaphtheirein ta ōa], lay snares for their offspring and destroy their own eggs.
